The mathematical verdict on Lemma1, Theorem2 and Corollary3 is PASS relative to n1's exact premises, without modifying the paper. The domain and raw mass are those in n1. For actual u,v in E1 define rho_j=MA(u^[n-j],v^[j]), d=v-u on finite-value representatives, D_j=int d(rho_j-rho_{j+1}), and I=sum D_j=int d(MA(u)-MA(v)). These numbers are finite by O, even when the potentials have literal poles. This is signed raw recursion, not a probability normalization.

For continuous endpoints Q_j=theta_u^(n-1-j)theta_v^j and rho_j-rho_{j+1}=-dd^c d Q_j. Thus D_j=D_Qj(d,d)>=0. Smooth Stokes gives D_Q(a,a)=int da wedge d^c a Q>=0; symmetry and positivity of D_Q(a+tb,a+tb) give Cauchy-Schwarz. Uniform semipositive regularization passes this to continuous differences: each signed curvature product expands into finitely many positive products of fixed intersection masses, hence has uniformly bounded total variation. Uniform convergence of a multiplying function and weak convergence of those products pass its integral, by splitting the error into the supnorm-times-TV error and a fixed continuous test. This verifies the actual continuous domain, rather than postulating singular test curvature on another bundle.

Write a real PL test f=h-k, with h,k FS metrics on the same ample rational A, as in n1. The two positive measures dd^c h Q_j and dd^c k Q_j both have raw mass (A.L^(n-1)). Therefore 0<=D_Qj(f,f)<=||f||_infinity ||dd^c f Q_j||_TV<=2||f||_infinity(A.L^(n-1))=:C_f. Cauchy-Schwarz gives |int f(rho_j-rho_{j+1})|^2<=C_f D_j. No ordering of u,v is required.

For singular endpoints use independent continuous nets u_a downarrow u and v_b downarrow v on the product directed set. Expand each D_j into exactly four weighted integrals: int v_b rho_j - int u_a rho_j - int v_b rho_{j+1} + int u_a rho_{j+1}. Every weight and every curvature slot is decreasing on that product. O passes each weighted integral separately to its finite limit. Hence their signed sum has a nonnegative limit D_j. Weak convergence passes the fixed continuous f tests, and the same C_f bound survives. This is not an application of a theorem to the nonmonotone difference v_b-u_a. Telescoping the signed measures, then finite Cauchy-Schwarz, gives |int f(MA(u)-MA(v))|^2<=n C_f I. V remains the original intersection mass throughout.

Let u_t=(1-t)u+tv and g(t)=E(u_t). O's finite affine energy polynomial and derivative, or the preceding four-integral coefficient passage, give -g''(t)=n sum_{j=0}^{n-1} binom(n-1,j)t^j(1-t)^(n-1-j)D_j. Define B_u(v)=E(u)-E(v)+int(v-u)MA(u), and reverse u,v for B_v(u). Integrating g'' twice gives B_u(v)=int_0^1(1-t)(-g'')dt and B_v(u)=int_0^1 t(-g'')dt. Repeated elementary integration by parts yields int_0^1 t^a(1-t)^b dt=a!b!/(a+b+1)! for nonnegative integers. Thus B_u(v)=sum (n-j)D_j/(n+1), B_v(u)=sum (j+1)D_j/(n+1). Consequently I/(n+1)<=B_u(v)<=nI/(n+1) and B_u(v)+B_v(u)=I. There is no missing factorial or mass factor.

For Delta=g(1/2)-(g(0)+g(1))/2 take G(t)=min(t,1-t)/2. G is zero at the endpoints and its derivative jumps by -1 at 1/2. Piecewise integration by parts gives Delta=int G(-g'')=sum alpha_{n,j}D_j with alpha_{n,j}=n binom(n-1,j)int G(t)t^j(1-t)^(n-1-j)dt. All alpha are positive. Here is an all-n proof of the exact minimum, independent of finite computations. Put b_{m,j}=binom(m,j)t^j(1-t)^(m-j). Symmetry gives alpha_j=alpha_{n-1-j}. From b'_{n,j+1}=n(b_{n-1,j}-b_{n-1,j+1}) and integration against G, alpha_{j+1}-alpha_j=(int_0^(1/2)b_{n,j+1}-int_(1/2)^1 b_{n,j+1})/2. If j+1<=n/2, then b(t)/b(1-t)=(t/(1-t))^(2(j+1)-n)>=1 on 0<t<=1/2. Therefore the alpha increase toward their middle and then decrease by symmetry, so the minimum occurs at an endpoint. To evaluate it, use the formal polynomial g=-(1-t)^(n+1)/(n+1), whose -g''=n(1-t)^(n-1). Its midpoint deficit is (1/2-2^(-(n+1)))/(n+1)=(1-2^(-n))/(2(n+1))=:c_n. This proves the stated exact minimum for every integer n>=1, including every retained n>=2. Thus Delta>=c_n I and |int f(MA(u)-MA(v))|^2<=n C_f Delta/c_n. This formal polynomial is an algebraic coefficient calculation, not an example of an actual metric.

If I=0 then all nonnegative D_j vanish. The individual PL estimate makes each rho_j-rho_{j+1} annihilate the real PL tests. Uniform density and TV<=2V extend this to every continuous test and identify the signed Radon measure as zero. Conversely equal pure measures make the defining finite integral I zero. Positivity of alpha makes Delta=0 equivalent to I=0. Hence zero I, zero Delta, equality of pure measures and equality of all successive mixed measures are equivalent. These are measure statements; they do not determine potential values at points or common poles.

For a common pure-measure fibre, the curvature binomial formula and equality of successive mixed measures show that every segment remains in the fibre. Induction gives every finite convex combination. For w1,...,wn in that fibre, form w_S=|S|^-1 sum_{i in S}w_i for every nonempty subset S. O's polarization is MA(w1,...,wn)=1/n! sum_{S nonempty}(-1)^(n-|S|)|S|^n MA(w_S). The coefficients sum to one because inclusion-exclusion counts onto maps from n labels to n labels: sum_{S}(-1)^(n-|S|)|S|^n=n!. This is valid also with repeated slots. Subset averages are actual E1 by convexity; weights are positive, zero curvature coefficients are omitted at poles, and no empty-subset potential or zero-times-infinity is evaluated. Thus every mixed output of fibre elements equals the common pure measure.

For Corollary3, only after a genuine solution MA(u)=mu is given, O gives its all-test integrability and M gives finite dual and attainment F_mu(u)=J. Then epsilon_mu(v)=J-F_mu(v)=B_u(v). The coefficient bounds imply I/(n+1)<=epsilon_mu(v)<=nI/(n+1), and the pure PL estimate gives |int f(MA(v)-mu)|^2<=n(n+1)C_f epsilon_mu(v). Mixed outputs of actual solutions equal mu by the fibre result. This is a conditional bound at an existing solution, not an inverse construction.

The coverage table independently accounts for equations (3)-(11), all coefficient, zero-defect, density, pole and fibre claims in the unchanged paper and its parallel argument. Finite diagnostics are separately recorded in n4. Artifacts: audit-report.json and proof-unit-coverage.json. The mathematical verdict on Theorem4, Proposition5, reference covariance and the retained scope is PASS relative to n1 and n2. For an intrinsic positive Radon target mu of raw mass V, all actual E1 scalars are absolutely mu-integrable and J is finite. Constants cancel in F_mu=E-int u mu because E(u+c)=E(u)+cV. M identifies the continuous and all-E1 suprema, so epsilon_mu(u)=J-F_mu(u)>=0 is finite. The zero potential has F=0, hence J>=0.

The integral term of F is affine on every actual E1 segment. Its midpoint deficit equals Delta(u,v), and F(midpoint)<=J gives Delta<=(epsilon(u)+epsilon(v))/2. By n2, for every real PL f, |int f(MA(u)-MA(v))|^2<=[nC_f/(2c_n)](epsilon(u)+epsilon(v)). This proves equation (14) with its precise factor two.

Choose continuous tests u_k with epsilon(u_k)<=1/k from the finite real supremum. This is an ordinary real-supremum selection, not a cofinal sequence for FS nets or the analytic carrier. Equation (14) makes their output integrals Cauchy on each PL test. For any f in C(T), choose a PL p uniformly close; the difference error against two positive mass-V outputs is at most 2V||f-p||. Their f-integrals are therefore Cauchy. Limits define a linear positive functional L on C(T), with |L(f)|<=V||f|| and L(1)=V. The ordinary compact Hausdorff positive-functional Riesz theorem applies exactly: L is represented by a unique finite positive regular Radon measure lambda of mass V. No metrizability, separability, first countability or countable cofinality is used.

Compare any other maximizing net u_i to the fixed sequence u_k. For a fixed PL f and tolerance, first make epsilon(u_k) and the sequence's scalar limit error small, then choose a tail with epsilon(u_i) small in (14). This proves its f-integrals have the same limit. Uniform density and common mass then give weak convergence for every continuous test on any directed net. Comparing one fixed u to the sequence and letting its error tend to zero yields equation (12): |int f(MA(u)-lambda)|^2<=[nC_f/(2c_n)]epsilon(u). Thus the common weak output limit is unique and independent of the maximizing net; no potential limit has been constructed.

To show lambda is intrinsic, work solely in M's selected original reference. Sup-normalize one maximizing sequence by finite constants; actual E1 endpoints have a finite supremum. Constants preserve F and epsilon. A tail satisfies F>=-1 since J>=0. With finite U=U_mu, d_n=n(n+1)/2, C=U(1+2M0), a=U sqrt(2d_n), M gives -1<=-B+C+a sqrt(B). Setting s=sqrt(B)>=0 yields s^2-a s-(C+1)<=0 and therefore B<=R=[(a+sqrt(a^2+4(C+1)))/2]^2. This is the exact root, including U=0; no reference moment alone or arbitrary mass-correct target is used for coercivity.

For any actual normalized w in E1, O's all-test bound with all n slots equal to u_k gives int(-w)MA(u_k)<=H_n[B(w)+nB(u_k)]<=H_n[B(w)+nR]. The function -w is nonnegative lower semicontinuous because w is upper semicontinuous, and it may be infinite at poles. The following argument validates the passage for arbitrary compact Hausdorff positive Radon measures, rather than assuming a metric-space version. For g>=0 lower semicontinuous and a finite positive Radon measure nu, its integral is the supremum of int h dnu over continuous 0<=h<=g. Indeed choose a finite level step approximation from below to min(g,N), choose inner compact subsets in its finitely many strict open superlevels, and use normality to construct continuous cutoff functions equal to one on those compact sets and supported in the corresponding superlevels. The sum of the step heights times these cutoffs is a continuous minorant of g; inner regularity makes its integral arbitrarily close to the step integral. Refine the levels and let N grow. Consequently weak convergence nu_i to nu gives int g dnu<=liminf_i int g dnu_i, since each fixed continuous minorant passes through weak convergence. This argument works for nets and uses only positivity, normality and Radon regularity. Applying it to g=-w proves equation (13).

Finite constant shifts recover absolute integrability of every unnormalized actual E1 scalar against lambda. Only now, after positivity, Radon regularity, raw mass V and all-E1 integrability are established, is M applied to lambda. It gives its finite J and intrinsic status. Directly from (13), U_lambda<=H_n(1+nR); M also gives J(lambda)<=U_lambda(1+2M0)+(d_n/2)U_lambda^2. Neither integrability nor this dual bound assumes lambda is an actual output. This order of argument avoids the missing inverse.

For mixed maximizing-net limits choose n slots from finitely many maximizing nets on their product directed set. Every nonempty subset average is actual E1 and, by concavity, has error at most the average of the chosen slots' errors; this tends to zero on that product. Each corresponding pure output tends to lambda. O's finite subset polarization, with coefficient sum one as proved in n2, then gives convergence of the genuine mixed output to lambda. Repeated slots and poles cause no additional operation beyond the admissible positive subset averages and omission of zero coefficients. A constant maximizing net proves any actual maximizer has pure output lambda; its mixed outputs have the same measure by the fibre result. An already known genuine solution is a maximizer by M, and only in that conditional case does its constant output show lambda=mu.

For another continuous psh reference psi'=psi+b, b is a finite bounded continuous scalar. Absolute potentials correspond as u'=u-b. O gives E_psi'(u')=E_psi(u)-E_psi(b), hence F_psi',mu(u')=F_psi,mu(u)-E_psi(b)+int b dmu. The same finite scalar corrects J, leaving epsilon unchanged. Absolute genuine outputs are unchanged; corresponding maximizing nets have the same lambda. This establishes reference independence without moving M's atoms or asserting its selected-reference moment at another reference. Equation (13) remains explicitly confined to the selected reference.

For Proposition5 all integrals int(v-u)[MA(u)-mu] are finite on common finite-value sets by O and the intrinsic target condition. The actual segment derivative of F at t=0 is that integral. If u maximizes, this one-sided derivative is nonpositive for every actual E1 competitor v. Conversely concavity gives F(v)-F(u)<=that derivative, so the inequalities imply F(u) is the all-E1 supremum and hence equals J by M. Equation (15) is exactly this equivalence. The directions are toward psh competitors; both signs of every continuous test need not be admissible. Density of PL tests therefore cannot change the inequalities into equality of measures.

The three original gaps remain OPEN: (i) actual E1 maximizing-potential attainment for every intrinsic target; (ii) lambda_mu=mu for every target, or a complete actual envelope/orthogonality/both-sign differentiation replacement proving it; (iii) I(u,v)=0 implies u=v+c at EVERY analytic point for one finite constant, including common poles, hence EVERY-solution EVERY-point uniqueness. If (i) and (ii) held, a constant maximizing net would give MA(u)=mu; if (iii) also held, solutions would be unique in the required sense. The paper proves neither premise. Its zero-defect result is only measure equality. Finite-U coercivity does not prove actual psh closure or potential compactness; weak measure limits do not supply potentials; C comparison and D descent do not fill these gaps. T's trivial-field and S's all-genus curve sectors are existing grants, with no n>=2 extrapolation. No missing envelope or model theorem, abstract closure or inverse-defined operator is imported. The full original P16.4 remains OPEN and candidate=false.
